s.a-device-downloads-an-acl-only.f7c29ae.source: A device downloads an ACL only when it does not already hold it, and the name carries ISE’s own hash of the contents — so the one your busiest group uses all day may have been fetched once, months ago, and never since, while a rarely used one is fetched afresh every few hours as it falls out of the device’s cache. The logins name it either way.

s.a-device-fetches-an-acl-only.8da83e6c.source: A device fetches an ACL only when it does not already hold it: this one it has held throughout. s.a-dump-of-the-database-once.9d294c32.source: A dump of the database once a day, made by its own engine’s own program: pg_dump on PostgreSQL, mariadb-dump on MariaDB, and on the file SQLite’s own backup, which is the file. It is consistent even while this is writing to it, and a fraction of the size of the database. A dump goes back into the engine it came off; what goes into any of the three is a copy, which the card below makes. If the client program is not on this machine a portable copy is made instead, so a night is never without one.

s.a-second-firewall-kept-saying-exactly..source: A second firewall, kept saying exactly the same thing as the first. This is for a pair in high availability: whichever of the two is carrying the traffic at any moment has to already hold every address the other does, so both are written to in the same pass rather than one being filled when it takes over. They share the list names and every rule on this page — it is one blacklist on two machines, not two blacklists. What they do not share is how they are reached: each has its own address, its own account, its own port and its own ssh key. One of them refusing does not stop the other being written to, and the Firewall page says which one is behind.

s.a-site-running-non-persistent-desktops.source: A site running non-persistent desktops — Horizon instant clones and their like — rebuilds thousands of computer accounts a day, and every one of them is an account created, an account changed and a directory object written. It is the machinery running, and on a page of things worth looking at it is the only thing anybody can see. ​Switched on, events of THAT SHAPE are marked as machinery and left out of the cards and the alarms. The shape is deliberately narrow: a MACHINE account doing something to a COMPUTER account or to a machine’s own service-connection point. A PERSON doing any of it is still drawn, a machine account put into a group that runs the domain is still drawn, the audit log being cleared is still drawn, and every event is read, kept and searchable either way. ​It hides the noise, not the threats.

s.every-ban-of-each-source-switched.8323.source: Every ban of each source switched on here is let go. An address banned by another source as well stays, for that one. With every source on, everybody is let back in.

s.every-ban-says-what-made-it.3a4389cf.source: Every ban says what made it. One list of banned addresses goes to the firewalls, into the published list and into the access list, made of the bans of every source switched on here. Switched off, a source makes no new bans and the ones it made are carried nowhere - they are kept, and run out as they would, and switched on again they are back. An address banned by two sources is carried while either is on. Only addresses on the internet are banned by the sources that count logins at devices, at the firewall or at the domain: the bans go to a firewall in front of the network.

Where its log is is the folder the syslog server files it in - or one file - and which files are its, as a pattern: *.log takes them all, and a server that writes one file a day is followed the way the NPS files are, the newest two. s.every-security-event-read-off-the.d8ac.source: Every Security event read off the controllers - the refusals, the lockouts, the sign-ins, the accounts and groups being changed, and everything read out of the directory. On a busy domain this is far bigger than everything else here put together. Nothing is ever judged by it and no address is ever banned for it, so erasing it lets nobody in and keeps nobody out - the Domain page simply starts again from whatever arrives next. The daemon carries on from where it is in each file rather than reading them again: on a domain writing millions a day, reading them again is not something anybody wants by accident.

s.every-sign-in-that-did-not.a2665b59.source: Every sign-in that did not get through the token server, newest first — both kinds. A wrong number twice and right the third time is somebody typing while it changed; the same account failing all day is a token out of step with the clock or an account with nothing enrolled. And the ones marked in orange are the other kind: the number was RIGHT and the sign-in was refused anyway, by the RADIUS server in front of the token software, for a reason of its own — a group the account is not in, a directory it could not reach. Those rows say so, and there is nothing wrong with the token on them. None of it is ever judged: the address on these records is the machine that asked, which is the token server itself.

s.everything-above-the-ending-is-this.66.source: Everything above the ending is this machine's: one deny line per address, written afresh every time. The ending is yours, and it is the same body of an access list you would type at the router — as many lines as your own list needs. Every line is read before it is saved, and a line a router would refuse is refused here instead, where it costs nothing. An access list ends with an implicit deny, so a list with no permit at the bottom is a list that stops everything: that is why this is a setting and not something to remember by hand.

s.everything-being-read-as-one-line.2150.source: Everything being read, as one line of time. Each bar is split by the door it came through — the VPN at the bottom, then TACACS+, the network, and the token server and the visitors’ network above those. Where the domain controllers are being read, what they refused stands beside them in blue, on the same scale — a refusal is a refusal whoever wrote it down. What they LET THROUGH has a scale of its own on the right, because one person signing in once writes several records on a controller and on one ruler it would bury everything else. s.firewall-kept-saying-exactly-the-same..source: firewall, kept saying exactly the same thing as the first. This is for a pair in high availability: whichever of the two is carrying the traffic at any moment has to already hold every address the other does, so both are written to in the same pass rather than one being filled when it takes over. They share the list names and every rule on this page — it is one blacklist on two machines, not two blacklists. What they do not share is how they are reached: each has its own address, its own account, its own port and its own ssh key.

s.gives-the-space-back-to-the.e82609f6.source: Gives the space back to the DISK. Deleting rows frees room inside the database file and the engine reuses it; nothing hands it back to the operating system until the whole thing is rebuilt. All three do that the same way — SQLite's VACUUM, MariaDB's OPTIMIZE TABLE, PostgreSQL's VACUUM FULL — and all three hold the table shut while they do it and need room for a second copy of the biggest one. Worth doing after throwing a lot away, and not otherwise.

s.how-long-the-successful-sign-ins.78b14.source: How long the successful sign-ins and sign-outs are kept, where that is SHORTER than the line above. ​0 means they are kept exactly as long as everything else, which is what this did before there was a number here. ​This is the middle answer between keeping them and not, and on most sites it is the RIGHT one. What this page is for - the refusals, the lockouts, the accounts and groups being changed - is worth three months, because "when did this start" is a question somebody really asks. Every machine in the building signing in is not. But when somebody presses an alarm and asks for the whole story of an account, the sign-ins and sign-outs around it are the context that makes the story readable - who was on that machine, whether they got in afterwards - and a site that switched them off has the alarm without the answer. Seven days here against ninety above keeps every investigation anybody actually does, and costs a fraction of the room. ​Anything this program has MARKED is kept for the full time whatever this says, so no alarm ever loses the events behind it. A number longer than the one above does nothing: nothing outlives that one.

s.how-often-to-ask-the-directory.97ffb8e.source: How often to ask the directory again about the people who are already signed in . What somebody may do here is worked out from their groups at the moment they sign in, and a sign-in lasts hours: without this, taking an administrator out of the administrators’ group leaves them an administrator until their sign-in runs out. At this interval each of them is looked up again — if their groups now earn the other role, the account is changed and their sign-ins end, so the next one comes back as what they now are; if their groups earn nothing, or the account has gone or been switched off in the directory, their sign-ins end and they cannot get back in. A directory that cannot be reached changes nothing, because an outage is not an answer about anybody. 0 never asks again, and a role then lasts as long as the sign-in does.

At a chosen hour lines up whatever is fetched daily or less often with the time below — for the one case it is for: the country database is about a hundred megabytes, and pulling that down somebody’s line in the middle of the working day is a choice. s.keeps-what-the-directory-says-about.fb.source: Keeps what the directory says about itself AS IT IS NOW, and weighs every later reading against it. ​The one change worth waking somebody for is not in any log: an account that is in the group which runs the domain this morning and was not in it last night. Only the directory knows, and only against what it said before. Switched on, the Domain page grows a Remember button; press it and who is in each of those groups, how many accounts a service runs as, after how many wrong passwords the domain locks, what it will accept as encryption, which machines are its controllers and which domains it trusts are all written down. Anything that moves after that is red on that page, says what it was and when it changed, and puts a band across the top of every page here until somebody either switches this off or remembers what the directory says now. ​READ ONLY, like everything else here: what is remembered is written into THIS database and never into Active Directory.

s.nps-writes-a-switch-port-down.ccdd62c4.source: NPS writes a switch port down as the switch’s own number for it — 50124 is stack member 1, port 24 — and never as its name, so whether it is Gigabit, Fast or Ten Gigabit is not in the log. Say it here and the ports are written the way ISE writes them: GigabitEthernet1/0/24. One name is every switch’s. Switches that differ are named by a pattern, comma separated, first match wins: SW_OLD_*=FastEthernet, SW_CORE*=TenGigabitEthernet, GigabitEthernet. Empty shows the number alone: 1/0/24. Changing it rewrites the ports already stored, in place.

Replication is the one everybody meets first: the three rights behind it are how every password in a domain is read at once, which is worth an alarm from a member server and is simply what two controllers do all day. ​THE SHORT NAME IS ENOUGH: write “dc01” and “DC01$”, “DC01.example.com” and “EXAMPLE\DC01$” are all understood as the same machine. An address on its own works too — the machine at it is looked up here. ​Left EMPTY the whole list is worked out rather than asked for: the controllers these logs come from, the directory servers this signs in against, and the machines the domain itself says are its controllers. Fill it in to say so exactly.

Unencrypted: the password crosses the network in the clear - only on a network that is yours alone. s.routeros-does-not-write-what-became.54.source: RouterOS does not write what became of a packet, only the log prefix of the rule that logged it. A prefix with DROP, REJECT, DENY, BLOCK, BAN or TARPIT in it is a refusal and one with ACCEPT, ALLOW, PERMIT or PASS a pass whatever this says; a NAT rule and one whose action goes on to the next rule (add-src-to-address-list, mark-connection, jump) are only said. Every other line - no prefix, LOG-FORWARD, OVPN - is a rule that only logs or lets through with log=yes: allow takes it as let through (a packet a logging DROP rule then refused in the same second is counted once, as that refusal), info only says it. A packet the router found invalid is only said either way. Choose info if a rule that refuses without logging stands behind a rule that only logs.

s.the-logs-say-what-happened-the.d652402.source: The logs say what happened; the directory says what it happened TO, and only the two together say whether anybody should care. Switched on, a handful of small searches a day against each directory that is set up here answer the questions no log can: ​which accounts a SERVICE runs as — a ticket asked for in RC4 is kerberoasting against one of those and an old application against anything else; which accounts have their pre-authentication switched off on purpose — a ticket asked for without it is ordinary against those and is somebody trying every account in turn against the rest; which accounts are switched off altogether — something still trying one of those is something nobody told; and who is in the groups that run the domain, following groups inside groups, so that an account being hammered is weighed by what it can actually do. ​Where any of that makes an alarm worse, the alarm gets worse and says in words which fact did it. ​IT READS AND NEVER WRITES. Nothing is ever changed in Active Directory, by this or by anything else in this program; a directory that will not answer leaves what was known exactly as it was; and with no directory set up this does nothing at all. What it last found is on the Domain page.

s.the-same-file-with-everything-in.b6498.source: The same file with everything in it: both passwords, the private half of the ssh key that reaches the router, the domain’s certificate, the key in the published ban list’s URL, and every account’s password as it is kept here. A machine built from this one needs nothing typed in at all. Which database to use is never carried — each machine keeps its own — and neither file holds anything read from the logs. It is also a file that gets somebody into your firewall, so it belongs where passwords belong and nowhere else.

s.the-same-for-objects-being-read.b3e4e0.source: The same for objects being read out of the directory, where that is SHORTER than the line above, and 0 for "as long as everything else". ​The half of the volume nobody ever looks at, and the one where a week is almost always plenty: what a read is ever wanted for is "what happened around this incident", and an incident nobody has noticed in a week is an incident nobody is going to. A read worth knowing about - a member server asking to replicate every password - is marked when it is read and is kept for the full time regardless.

s.what-somebody-may-do-here-is.7a2e8d01.source: . What somebody may do here is worked out from their groups at the moment they sign in, and a sign-in lasts hours: without this, taking an administrator out of the administrators’ group leaves them an administrator until their sign-in runs out. At this interval each of them is looked up again — if their groups now earn the other role, the account is changed and their sign-ins end, so the next one comes back as what they now are; if their groups earn nothing, or the account has gone or been switched off in the directory, their sign-ins end and they cannot get back in. A directory that cannot be reached changes nothing, because an outage is not an answer about anybody.

A NAT rule logs a connection’s first packet before it is translated, so the address is the one the router’s other lines show for that way out (≈), the port kept as RouterOS keeps it when it can - and for a dst-nat, the server inside that the filter’s lines show connections to that address and port going to (≈ →). A FortiGate’s and an FTD’s translations are written in their sessions: here is every session that was translated, with what its source was made and where its destination was sent (← the address it was asked at). The sessions themselves, with the translation each was given, are under Sessions.

s.whether-a-successful-sign-in-is.364455.source: Whether a SUCCESSFUL sign-in is kept at all — and the sign-out that follows it, the ticket behind it, and the programs started under it. ​On a busy domain this is most of everything there is: on one real domain, of 756,000 events in a day, 500,000 were sign-ins. Every person signing in once writes a Kerberos ticket, an NTLM validation and a logon, and every service they open writes another; every machine in the building does the same all day. Every one of those is followed by a sign-out, which is why the sign-outs are under this switch and not one of their own — they exist only because the sign-in did, and a domain that has stopped keeping one has not asked to keep the other. ​Switched off, they are read, weighed and thrown away instead of being written down. THE ALARMS DO NOT DEPEND ON THEM: anything this program has marked is kept whichever way this is set, and refusals, lockouts, and accounts and groups being changed are a different switch entirely (there is none - those are always kept). ​BUT READ THIS BEFORE SWITCHING IT OFF. What goes with them is not just the Logins page’s "Active Directory" tab. It is the sign-ins and sign-outs AROUND an incident - who was on that machine when the lockout happened, whether the account got in afterwards, what else that session did - which is exactly what somebody wants when they press an alarm and ask for the whole story of an account. The alarm is still there; the context around it is not. ​Which is why, on most sites, the answer is not this switch at all: leave it ON and give it a SHORT number of days below. Seven days of sign-ins against ninety of everything else keeps every investigation anybody actually does - nobody looks into last March’s morning - and costs a fraction of the room. Switching it off altogether is for a domain so large that even a week of them is too much. ​It changes nothing about what has already been stored; Settings → The database throws that away.

s.whether-a-tac-plus-server-s.b52458cf.source: Whether a tac_plus server’s logs are read at all. Off is the default and off is the whole of it: no file is opened, no button appears and nothing else here behaves differently. On, what it wrote is shown beside what ISE wrote — who signed in to which switch, from where, and every command they ran — under a TAC_Plus button of its own on the refusals and on the logins. Nothing read here earns a ban unless Logins to network devices is switched on under Banning, and then only from an address on the internet: the address on one of these lines is as often as not a jump host the whole of the network staff comes through.

s.whether-a-windows-nps-server-s.f364423.source: Whether a Windows NPS server’s logs are read at all. Off is the default and off is the whole of it: no file is opened, no button appears and nothing else here behaves differently. On, what NPS answered is shown beside what ISE answered, under buttons of its own — NPS VPN, NPS 802.1X LAN, NPS 802.1X Wi-Fi, NPS MAB LAN and NPS MAB Wi-Fi — and each of those appears only once NPS has really answered something through it. The switches’ own “is the server there” probes are recognised and left out. Only a VPN refusal is ever judged, while The VPN through a Windows NPS under Banning is on; a socket or a radio never earns a ban.

s.whether-the-domain-page-s-answers.b267.source: Whether the Domain page’s answers are counted as the events arrive rather than worked out afresh every time somebody looks. ​On, which is what a new installation gets: every card on that page is "in this window, the busiest twelve accounts / machines / addresses, and how many of each", and asked of the events themselves that is a walk of the whole window - on a domain of seven and a half million events a day, two to five seconds EACH, four cards to a page. Counted as they arrive it is a sum over a handful of rows, and the cost is set by how many accounts the DOMAIN has rather than by how many events it has written: on one real day, 48 events to a counted row, and that only improves as the traffic grows. ​The counting is written in the same transaction as the events, so the two cannot part company - and it is read back against them every hour anyway. If they ever disagree the page goes straight back to asking the events themselves, says so in the log, and nobody is shown a wrong number. ​Off is that older way for everything, and costs nothing but speed.

s.whether-the-ise-logs-are-read.0d1b66c4.source: Whether the ISE logs are read at all. On, because this program was written around them. Off is for an installation that has no ISE — a token server on its own, eduroam on its own, a tac_plus of your own: no ISE file is opened, and the VPN, TACACS and 802.1X/MAB buttons are not offered on Failed attempts or on Logins, so those two lists open on a door that something is actually arriving through. It stops the reading and the offering and nothing else. Everything already written down stays where it is, is still searched and still counted, and switching this back on shows it again — nothing anywhere is deleted by a switch. With this off, nobody can earn a ban from a VPN refusal, because there are no VPN refusals arriving to earn one.

s.whether-the-traffic-page-s-cards.2c40d.source: Whether the Traffic page’s cards, chart and lists of the busiest are worked out behind the daemon and kept ready, so that the page opens at once. On a big firewall they are sums over millions of counted buckets, and worked out while somebody waits that was minutes for the first look. s.which-name-servers-to-ask-in.c3a2edaf.source: Which name servers to ask, in the order to ask them: 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2 , or one per line, each with :port after it where it is not 53. The first one that hands over a name is the answer and the rest are not asked. A server that does not answer, refuses, or says it has never heard of the address is passed over rather than believed — a site keeps its offices in one set of servers and its DMZ in another, and the first one having no record of an address says nothing about whether the second one has. This machine’s own resolver is never used: it holds one answer to a question that has several.

s.which-zone-to-read-a-log.fe518def.source: Which zone to read a log line that carries none. ISE writes the offset that was in force on every record — +02:00 — so nothing here touches the ISE logs, and none of this can move a VPN attempt by a second. The token log and the eduroam log write Sep 25 10:21:25 and nothing else, and a time like that is not a moment until somebody says where it was written: read in the wrong zone it is not refused, it is simply hours out, which is the one kind of wrong that looks right. Empty reads it in this machine’s own zone, which is what a site whose clocks agree wants and what this has always done. Set it where they do not agree, as a name out of the zone database — Europe/Prague , which knows when summer time starts — or as a fixed offset: +02:00 . Records already written keep the times they were written with; erasing that log’s records reads them again.

s.whole-countries-that-are-never-kept.f0.source: Whole countries that are never kept out, by the same country database that puts the flags on this page. An address in one of them is recorded and counted and never banned — not by the counting, not by a public list, not by a name that was never an account. It is for the country your own people dial in from, where a wrong password at six in the morning should never lock somebody out of their own VPN. It is a blunt instrument: everybody else in that country is spared too, and somebody attacking from inside it is spared with them. Anything already banned in a country added here is let back in at the same moment.

r.a-refusal-at-the-vpn-through.cefa0019.source:
A refusal at the VPN through a Windows NPS - a FortiGate, an ASA or any gateway that asks NPS about a password - is counted and banned exactly as a refusal at the VPN through ISE is: the same bar, the same window, the same ladder.

NPS says which requests are a VPN by itself: the gateway asks on a Virtual port and for a network, not for a shell at a switch’s prompt. Wi-Fi and the sockets in the building are never judged. The list of devices under Logs is ISE’s and does not apply here. An EAP conversation the machine walked away from decided nothing and is not counted.

r.a-second-directory-asked-only-who.4074.source:
A second directory, asked only who somebody is — and only about a name the first one does not have. It is for the site that signs its administrators in against one domain while the people in its ISE logs live in another.

r.a-second-firewall-kept-saying-exactly..source:
A second firewall, kept saying exactly the same thing as the first.

It is for a pair in high availability: whichever of the two is carrying the traffic at any moment has to already hold every address the other does, so both are written to in the same pass rather than one being filled when it takes over.

They share the list names and every rule on this page — it is one blacklist on two machines, not two blacklists. What they do not share is how they are reached: its own address, its own account, its own port and its own key. One of them refusing does not stop the other being written to, and the Firewall page says which one is behind.

r.attacks-arrive-from-whole-streets-this.source:
Attacks arrive from whole streets: this VPN sees thirty-two tries each from a dozen addresses in one /24. Folding turns those into one line, so the router carries one rule instead of a dozen and the list stays readable.

A subnet is only made where two or more banned addresses fall inside it, and never where it would swallow anything under never kept out. Everything kept about each address stays under its own name, and any folding can be undone on its own afterwards.

r.cisco-ftd-and-asa-are-read.7b307028.source: Cisco FTD and ASA are read from their own syslog messages - %FTD-6-302014: Teardown TCP connection… - however the syslog server files them: all in one file, or a file per message id (%FTD-6-302014.log), every one of which is followed. A session is counted once, when it ends, with how long it lasted, how much it carried (both ways together: FTD does not say which way) and why it ended; the line that opened it lends it its direction and its address translation. Refusals by access group or by a downloadable ACL, packets dropped on the way, the remote-access VPN and the site-to-site tunnels, failover, threat detection, and the management centre's file and intrusion events are all read. For a pair in failover give one firewall a folder for each unit: only the active unit's sessions are counted, and the standby's copies of them are left out. The time is the syslog header's, read in the zone of the firewall's clock - set beside each firewall below; an FTD writes UTC unless told otherwise, and one whose lines keep arriving whole hours old is said so here.

r.every-downloadable-acl-the-vpn-logins..source:
Every downloadable ACL the VPN logins were given, how many logins each one, and whether its rules are among the records kept here.

A device downloads an ACL only when it does not already hold it, and the name carries ISE’s own hash of the contents — so the one your busiest group uses all day may have been fetched once, months ago, and never since, while a rarely used one is fetched afresh every few hours as it falls out of the device’s cache. The logins name it either way.

That is why a login can say which firewall it was handed and still show no rules: nothing is missing here, the download simply happened before these logs. It appears the next time the device has to fetch it — after a reload, after the cache drops it, or as soon as the ACL is edited on ISE, which changes its name and forces a fresh download.

r.every-firewall-whose-log-is-read.d9c4c.source: Every firewall whose log is read, one row each. Name is what it is called here: the Traffic page switches between firewalls by it and shows it beside every line. Kind is which firewall writes the log, because each writes its own shape of line. Where its log is is the folder the syslog server files it in - or one file - and which files are its, as a pattern: *.log takes them all, and a server that writes one file a day is followed the way the NPS files are, the newest two. Lines read before a firewall had a name carry none: isemon --erase firewall reads them again with it.

r.everybody-ise-let-in-newest-first.be60.source:
Everybody ISE let in, newest first.

Click a row for the whole record: on a VPN login the authorisation profile, the directory groups, the policy that matched, and the firewall the session was handed — the downloadable ACL, drawn as rules rather than as one long line. That ACL arrives as a record of its own in the same log; it is not a login, so it is not listed as one.

On the TACACS side ISE writes two kinds: Authentication is somebody signing in, Authorization is a command they were allowed to run once in. The commands are shown inside the session they were typed in rather than beside it.

r.everything-being-kept-out-at-this.b573.source:
Everything being kept out at this moment, in three groups by how it got there.

An address that fails to sign in often enough inside the window is caught by the counting, and the firewall is told to drop it. One that a public list already names goes on the first time it fails here at all — it is on somebody else’s list of known-bad and it has now knocked on this door, which is two things rather than one. The third group is whatever somebody put there by hand.

Anything under never kept out is left alone whatever it does, and how long a ban lasts is in Settings.

r.everything-being-read-as-one-line.4d8b.source:
Everything being read, as one line of time — the refusals the banning is made of, and the sign-ins beside them so a burst can be read against whether anybody was actually getting in.

Each bar is split by the door: the VPN underneath, then TACACS+, the network, and the token server and the visitors’ network above those. Different systems with different people in front of them, so the height means everything in that hour and the colours say which door. Only the VPN is ever judged.

Downloadable ACLs, commands run on a switch and ISE’s notes about its own packet handling are nobody knocking, so they are not drawn. They are counted under Everything else on the Failed attempts page.

Press a bar to open that hour, or a door below to see that door’s own shape.

r.how-often-to-ask-the-directory.d579fc3.source: How often to ask the directory again about the people who are already signed in. What somebody may do here is worked out from their groups at the moment they sign in, and a sign-in lasts hours: without this, taking an administrator out of the administrators’ group leaves them an administrator until their sign-in runs out. At this interval each of them is looked up again — if their groups now earn the other role, the account is changed and their sign-ins end, so the next one comes back as what they now are; if their groups earn nothing, or the account has gone or been switched off in the directory, their sign-ins end and they cannot get back in. A directory that cannot be reached changes nothing, because an outage is not an answer about anybody. 0 never asks again, and a role then lasts as long as the sign-in does.

r.how-the-automatic-fetching-decides-whe.source: How the automatic fetching decides when to go. By the interval means what it says: something set to every hour is fetched every hour, something set to every 30 days every 30 days, and nothing else has an opinion about it. r.mikrotik-routeros-is-read-from-its.208.source: MikroTik RouterOS is read from its own syslog lines - a /system logging action of type remote pointed at this machine, and a rule for each topic wanted: firewall, system, account, ssh, ovpn, l2tp, sstp, dhcp. However the syslog server files them - all in one file, or a file per topic (firewall,info.log) - every file is followed. A firewall line says only that a rule logged the packet, never what became of it: that is read off the rule's log prefix - DROP, REJECT, DENY, BLOCK is a refusal, ACCEPT, ALLOW, PERMIT a pass, anything else is shown as logged. Sign-ins to the router (winbox, ssh, the web, the API), every change to its configuration and who made it, the VPN of people (OpenVPN, L2TP, SSTP, PPTP: who, from where, which address inside) and the tunnels to other sites are read as well; a refused sign-in from the internet can earn a ban like any other at the firewall. The time is the syslog header's, read in the zone set beside the firewall.

r.normally-a-record-is-weighed-as.5dd8ec.source:
Normally a record is weighed as it arrives, and one older than a day is written down but not acted on — which is what stops a machine installed on a Tuesday from banning half the internet for what it did in June.

This does the opposite, once, because you asked: every log is read from the beginning — the rotated copies beside it as well, so the days before this daemon was installed are read too — and everything in them is weighed by the rules as they stand now.

Nothing is stored twice: every record is kept under the session id ISE gave it, so one already here is recognised and left exactly as it is and only what was missing is added. The pass says both numbers when it finishes, so there is nothing to take on trust.

r.radius-log-does-not-say-which.2c1e043f.source: radius.log does not say which door a sign-in came through, so it is worked out: a calling station that is an address is the VPN, and so is anything through a client named below as the VPN; a name that is the machine's own MAC is MAB, everything else 802.1X; and LAN or Wi-Fi is the client's, as named below, or else what the accounting files said of that machine - its port type, or a network name on a radio. r.the-addresses-being-kept-out-published.source:
The addresses being kept out, published at a URL for a firewall this machine does not log in to: a Cisco FTD through its FMC, a FortiGate, or anything that reads a list of addresses. The firewall fetches it every few minutes by itself, so a ban made here reaches it on the next fetch and one that ends here leaves it on the fetch after that.

The addresses being kept out, published at a URL for a firewall this machine does not log in to: a Cisco FTD through its FMC, a FortiGate, or anything that reads a list of addresses. The firewall fetches it every few minutes by itself, so a ban made here reaches it on the next fetch and one that ends here leaves it on the fetch after that.

The URL needs no sign-in: whoever may reach it can read the list, and nothing else. Whitelisted addresses are never in it.

r.the-addresses-the-counting-can-see.77a.source:
The addresses the counting can see right now — inside the window and not yet out — and how far each one still has to go.

It is the half of the story this page never showed: an empty list above says nothing about whether nothing is happening or whether everything is happening one attempt below the line.

An address is counted from the end of its last ban: what it was banned for once is not charged to it again, so serving a ban and being let back in both start it again at nought.

Only attempts at the VPN are counted here. A machine failing 802.1X or MAB on a socket, or somebody mistyping a password on a switch over TACACS+, is recorded and shown on its own tab and can never earn anybody a ban — the address on such a record is usually the switch itself.

r.the-whole-configuration-as-one-json.70.source:
The whole configuration as one JSON file, to rebuild this machine somewhere else or to keep beside a backup.

There are two shapes of it. The plain one is safe to mail and to paste into a ticket: it has no passwords, no ssh key and no certificate in it, and a machine built from it comes up unable to reach the firewall or ask the domain anything until those are typed in.

The complete one has all of them, so a machine built from it needs nothing typed in at all — and is a file that gets into your firewall, so keep it the way you keep the keys themselves.

r.this-account-comes-from-the-directory..source:
This account comes from the directory. Its password is the domain’s and is never kept here; what it may do comes from its groups there, and is worked out afresh every time it signs in. Neither can be set on this page — the domain is where they are decided, and anything set here would be overwritten the next time they signed in.
This machine can still switch the account off, which stops it getting in whatever the domain says. That is the one lock that does not need a domain administrator.

r.which-name-servers-to-ask-in.a859b144.source: Which name servers to ask, in the order to ask them: 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2, or one per line, each with :port after it where it is not 53. The first one that hands over a name is the answer and the rest are not asked. A server that does not answer, refuses, or says it has never heard of the address is passed over rather than believed — a site keeps its offices in one set of servers and its DMZ in another, and the first one having no record of an address says nothing about whether the second one has. This machine’s own resolver is never used: it holds one answer to a question that has several.

r.which-zone-to-read-a-log.16da58d5.source: Which zone to read a log line that carries none. ISE writes the offset that was in force on every record — +02:00 — so nothing here touches the ISE logs, and none of this can move a VPN attempt by a second. The token log and the eduroam log write Sep 25 10:21:25 and nothing else, and a time like that is not a moment until somebody says where it was written: read in the wrong zone it is not refused, it is simply hours out, which is the one kind of wrong that looks right. Empty reads it in this machine’s own zone, which is what a site whose clocks agree wants and what this has always done. Set it where they do not agree, as a name out of the zone database — Europe/Prague, which knows when summer time starts — or as a fixed offset: +02:00. Records already written keep the times they were written with; erasing that log’s records reads them again.

r.whole-countries-that-are-never-kept.1f.source:
Whole countries that are never kept out, by the same country database that puts the flags on this page. An address in one of them is recorded and counted and never banned — not by the counting, not by a public list, not by a name that was never an account.

It is for the country your own people dial in from, where a wrong password at six in the morning should never lock somebody out of their own VPN. It is a blunt instrument: everybody else in that country is spared too, and somebody attacking from inside it is spared with them. Anything already banned in a country added here is let back in at the same moment.

Somebody who is not there falls back to the local accounts, which is what keeps a way in on the morning the directory is down.
